exercise1.prompt: A Cat that extends Animal, calling super() in both __init__ and make_sound

cases.name: Cat is built from Animal and writes its own __init__ and make_sound
cases.describe: a Cat class written as class Cat(Animal) with __init__ and make_sound

cases.name: the cat has the name the parent was meant to set

hiddenCases.name: the parent is reached through super, not by hand
Animal is the class that defines __init__ and make_sound first
hiddenCases.describe: an Animal class holding __init__ and make_sound

hiddenCases.name: the cat also has the colour Cat added
both sounds are printed, the parent's and then Meow
hiddenCases.describe: the parent's line followed by Meow

exercise1.hint: Writing __init__ in the child replaces the parent's entirely, so anything the parent used to set is simply never set. super().__init__(...) is how you get that work done before adding your own.

exercise2.prompt: A Manager that extends Employee, adding a team size to both __init__ and get_info

cases.name: Manager is built from Employee and writes its own __init__ and get_info
cases.describe: a Manager class written as class Manager(Employee) with __init__ and get_info

cases.name: the manager has the name the parent was meant to set

hiddenCases.name: the parent is reached through super, not by hand
Employee is the class that defines __init__ and get_info first
hiddenCases.describe: an Employee class holding __init__ and get_info

hiddenCases.name: the manager also has the team size Manager added
get_info carries the parent's information as well as the team size
hiddenCases.call: all(part in Manager("Sarah", "Project Manager", 4).get_info() for part in ["Sarah", "Project Manager", "4"])

exercise2.hint: The child's get_info is meant to extend the parent's answer, not replace it. Ask the parent first, keep what it returns, then add the part only Manager knows about.

questions.prompt: A subclass defines __init__ and never calls super().__init__(). What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, the parent runs first automatically
Anything the parent's __init__ set is never set at all
Python raises an error when the class is defined
questions.explain: Defining __init__ in the child replaces the parent's. Nothing runs it for you, so the parent's attributes simply do not exist.

choices: A new object of the parent class
A way to call the parent's version of a method on this same object
The name of the parent class as a string
A copy of the parent's attributes
questions.explain: No second object is made. super() reaches the parent's method and hands it the object you already have.

questions.prompt: Put the body of Manager.__init__ in the order that works.
questions.explain: Let the parent finish setting up what it owns, then add what only the child knows about.

questions.prompt: Which are true of super().get_info() inside Manager.get_info?
choices: It runs Employee's get_info on this same manager
It returns a value you can build on
It calls Manager's get_info again, forever
It creates a new Employee object
questions.explain: super() deliberately starts the lookup above the current class, which is what stops it finding itself and recursing.
